Waiting for Godot. Samuel Beckett's 1952 play—originally written in French as En attendant Godot—depicts two men, Vladimir and Estragon, waiting on a country road for someone named Godot, who never arrives. A defining work of the Theatre of the Absurd, it strips drama to its most spare elements: two characters, minimal plot, and dialogue that circles endlessly, capturing the hopelessness and dark humor of human existence.

First performed in Paris in 1953, it revolutionized modern drama by abandoning conventional plot, character development, and resolution. The central conceit is simple: two men wait for Godot across two acts, passing time with games, conversations, and philosophical riffs. Yet nothing materially changes between the acts, and this stasis becomes the play's meaning.

Famous for the line "Nothing to be done"—Vladimir's opening phrase—which becomes a refrain capturing the play's mood of stasis and futility. The play features only four characters: Vladimir and Estragon, the waiting pair; Pozzo and Lucky, a master and his servant who appear and disappear; and the absent Godot.

The play is a meditation on meaning, hope, friendship, and survival when no ultimate meaning is forthcoming. It reflects existential anxiety and the human need to create meaning through routine. Marked by minimalist language, repetitive structures, and a darkly comic tone, it allows the audience to laugh at despair itself. The work became an iconic text of the twentieth century, influencing countless writers and dramatists, and revived theatre's capacity for philosophical and formal innovation.
